item.title: Explicit HTTP Proxy Styles
item.description:
Proxy comparison #

Proxy behavior ↓ / Client → proxy hop → HTTP to proxy HTTPS to proxy
Forward proxy — client sends absolute-form requests, e.g. GET http://target/path Pros: Simplest and broadly supported; proxy can authenticate, cache, filter, route, and log HTTP requests; low protocol overhead. Cons: The client-to-proxy request, headers, URL, and body are plaintext unless the target payload is separately protected; unsafe across untrusted local networks. Pros: Encrypts the client-to-proxy hop, hiding proxy credentials and HTTP request details from the local network; proxy retains HTTP-aware capabilities after TLS terminates. Cons: More TLS setup/CPU cost; proxy still sees and can modify request contents; less universally deployed/configured than an HTTP proxy URL.
Tunnel proxy — client sends CONNECT host:port, then streams bytes Pros: Standard, widely compatible way to reach HTTPS origins through a proxy; end-to-end TLS remains between client and destination; proxy normally cannot inspect the HTTP payload. Cons: CONNECT request and destination host/port are plaintext on the client-to-proxy hop; proxy traffic is observable and may be blocked/limited; no HTTP caching or request-level policy without TLS interception. Pros: Encrypts both the CONNECT setup—including proxy authentication and destination authority—and the tunnel hop; with HTTPS inside the tunnel, provides layered protection across an untrusted local network. Cons: Two TLS layers and extra setup overhead; harder to debug and somewhat less compatible; proxy still observes connection metadata after decrypting its outer TLS layer, and policies remain mostly connection-level.

“HTTPS to proxy” means the proxy itself is reached over TLS—such as an https://proxy.example:443 proxy configuration. It is independent of whether the target site uses HTTPS.
